clinicalPearls: An aggressive mature T-cell leukaemia typically presenting with a very high lymphocyte count, hepatosplenomegaly and generalised lymphadenopathy
Skin infiltration and serous effusions are recognised and relatively distinctive extranodal features
The blood film shows small to medium prolymphocytes with a visible nucleolus and characteristic cytoplasmic blebbing or protrusions
The cells are usually mature T cells expressing CD2, CD3, CD5 and CD7, most often CD4 positive, and frequently co-express CD4 and CD8
Rearrangement or overexpression of the TCL1 oncogene, commonly through inversion or translocation of chromosome 14, is the defining molecular lesion
Association with ataxia-telangiectasia and somatic ATM abnormalities is well recognised
The course is usually rapidly progressive, and durable control generally requires monoclonal antibody therapy followed by allogeneic transplantation in fit patients
reference.pathophysiology: T-cell prolymphocytic leukaemia is a clonal malignancy of mature post-thymic T lymphocytes. The hallmark oncogenic event is aberrant activation of the TCL1 family of oncogenes, most often through chromosome 14 inversions or translocations that juxtapose TCL1 with T-cell receptor regulatory elements, driving proliferation via enhanced AKT signalling. Additional abnormalities of the ATM gene on chromosome 11, echoing the germline defect of ataxia-telangiectasia, impair DNA damage responses and contribute to genomic instability. The resulting rapidly dividing clone accumulates in blood, marrow, spleen, liver, lymph nodes and skin.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia with increased prolymphocytes
Mantle cell lymphoma in leukaemic phase
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood film to identify prolymphocyte morphology
Flow cytometry immunophenotyping including CD4/CD8 and TCL1 expression
Cytogenetics and FISH for chromosome 14 (TCL1) and chromosome 11 (ATM) abnormalities
T-cell receptor gene rearrangement to confirm clonality
Cross-sectional imaging to assess organomegaly and effusions
Bone marrow examination to document infiltration
redFlags: Rapidly doubling lymphocyte count with progressive organomegaly
Development of effusions or symptomatic skin infiltration
Marrow failure with cytopenias and infection or bleeding
Central nervous system or other extranodal spread
reference.prognosis: T-cell prolymphocytic leukaemia is aggressive with historically short survival; monoclonal antibody induction can produce remission, but long-term disease control usually depends on allogeneic transplantation in eligible patients.
pitfalls: Mislabelling it as an atypical B-cell chronic lymphocytic leukaemia without immunophenotyping
Adopting a watch-and-wait strategy suited to indolent disease in this aggressive entity
Overlooking TCL1 and ATM testing that confirm the diagnosis
Underestimating the poor prognosis when counselling and planning transplant early
management: Intravenous alemtuzumab, an anti-CD52 monoclonal antibody, as induction of choice to achieve remission
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation to consolidate remission in eligible, fit patients
Antimicrobial prophylaxis against Pneumocystis, cytomegalovirus and fungal infection during profound alemtuzumab-induced immunosuppression, with cytomegalovirus viral-load monitoring
Blood-product support and management of cytopenias and organomegaly-related symptoms
Consideration of novel agents or clinical trials, such as BCL2 inhibition, for relapsed or refractory disease
Regular monitoring for relapse given the high relapse rate after remission
Management within a specialist haematology and transplant centre
